newsitem.title: UK: New clues to cause of dementia in Aids sufferers.
newsitem.headline: New clues to cause of dementia in Aids sufferers.

text.p: Scientists investigating the cause of dementia in AIDS patients said on Wednesday they may have discovered how the virus gets into the brain.
Dana Gabuzda, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, said the new findings could have significant implications for the development of drugs to prevent or treat AIDS dementia.
AIDS develops when the HIV virus attacks a carrier's immune system. More than 3.1 million people contracted the disease last year, bringing the world total to around 30 million.
Between 20 and 30 percent of patients develop some sort of brain disease after full-blown AIDS sets in, suffering symptoms like memory loss and loss of bodily function, Gabuzda said in an interview.
But she said it was a relatively poorly understood aspect of the disease, as research tends to focus on the immune system.
The HIV virus is known to attack white blood cells using a variety of cell-surface receptors such as CD4.

Results from the five-strong Dana-Farber team, published in the scientific journal Nature, showed that both CCR3 and CCR5 receptors present in the brain could promote infection of the central nervous system by some strains of the HIV virus.
The scientists found that individuals with defective CCR5 exhibited resistance to HIV-1, suggesting that CCR5 plays an important role as a co-receptor in allowing the virus entry.
This finding marked the first proof that CCR3 plays a role in HIV infection and is likely to pave the way for further study, Gabuzda said.
Studies would now look at the possibility that CCR3 could be acting as a receptor elsewhere in the body, for example in the lungs or lymph nodes.

"The identification of CCR3 as a co-receptor contributing to efficient HIV-1 infection of microglia (the main target cells in the brain) may suggest new therapeutic strategies to inhibit HIV-1 replication in the central nervous system," Nature said.
A recent study of 2,600 AIDS patients published in the British Medical Journal showed median survival after diagnosis to be 20 months.
While a cure for AIDS remains a distant prospect, scientists say new drugs are delaying the development of full-blown AIDS in HIV-infected patients.
